events.text: An original stag beetle on weathered wood, sparked by the Natural History Museum stag beetle account: https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/stag-beetles.html . Practice: broad filled wing cases first, clear air between limbs and jaws, then a few compact reflections.
The green washes leave wide pale channels. I will cross them diagonally before placing the log, so the ground supports rather than stripes the insect.
Diagonal washes reduced the channels, though pale bands remain. A broad warm log will carry the beetle and give its dark legs a readable field.
The log is filled and diagonal, but the long bristle ridges are very regular. Broken grain and uneven warm planes can interrupt that rhythm without outlining every edge.
Broken grain is subtle against the original ridges. The next dark body masses need loaded paint and broad overlaps; the pale wood will remain visible between the later legs.
The shell is filled, but its upper left shoulder has a pale notch and the thorax has a pointed cap. I will bridge that notch broadly and give the head a shorter, flatter silhouette.

The warm left wing case reads against the dark right. Before highlights, six separated legs must establish the stance. I will place their bent upper sections first, keeping the wood visible between them.
The left legs stay distinct, but their turns are angular. Thin sampled extensions can soften the feet without thickening every joint. Two right legs will complete the stance first.
All six legs now read with open spaces. The hind feet still end as spikes, so four short curved extensions will give them contact before the open jaws are added.
The feet taper and the leg gaps remain clear. I will keep a broad green opening between two curved mahogany jaws, using sampled arcs rather than a sharp three-point bend.
The arcs are round, but they float above the head and nearly touch at their tips. I will join their lower roots to the head and reopen the top gap; this is a structural correction before detail.
Jaw roots now meet the head, and the right wing case has a warm plane. I am leaning up to check the tip opening and root joins before choosing the next marks.

The green tip repair changed color but left a raised oval, so repeated narrow covers would build more relief. I will leave that limitation visible and develop the paired shell planes and short antennae.
Warm planes now survive whole view, while the center seam is still broad and dark. I will keep that division and lift only short curved shoulders, then give the antennae unequal clubs.
The short shell arcs round the shoulders without closing the center seam. A cooler thorax plane and small dark eyes should separate the head from the jaws before the surrounding wood is developed.
The thorax has a cool shoulder and the eyes stay small. The log is still too uninterrupted, so I will add a few unequal bark breaks away from the insect rather than more shell lines.
The left bark split reads, while the upper-right split sits too close to a foot. I will keep the next moss patches away from the legs and use broad low green planes at the log ends.
Moss anchors both log ends, but each patch is a blunt mound. Four unequal loaded tips will break those silhouettes, leaving the larger quiet patches intact.
The moss tips add irregularity without competing with the shell. I am moving down to check the feet and lower wood before placing a fallen leaf in the quiet green corner.

The leaf reads as a quiet gold counterweight. The raised green oval still closes the jaw tips; I will test one flat acrylic cover across that small gap, then inspect it alone before any further repair.

The acrylic cover changes the tip color only faintly; the relief remains conspicuous. I will stop covering it and keep the next refinements to leaf veins and bark structure where new marks can add useful form.
The small leaf veins stay quiet at whole view. I will give the empty left wood one broken knot and keep its dark center smaller than any beetle plane.
The broken knot reads as wood without stealing focus. The log ends are still brush-shaped, so a few unequal bark fibers and moss stems will roughen those transitions.
The broken end fibers make the log less rectangular. The beetle legs are still flat black bands; short muted joint lights can describe their bends while leaving their dark contours intact.
Joint lights are mostly close-view details, which keeps the stance dark. I will add two quieter middle-joint lights and short lower shell turns, keeping the bottom darker than the shoulders.
The lower turns now round both wing cases, and the leg gaps remain open. One compact shoulder reflection deserves a single-mark check before the final refinement.

The small shell reflection holds at whole view without becoming a stripe. Final refinement: one eye fleck, a short leaf-fold light, and a quieter bark neighbor beside the crowded right foot; then I will review and stop if further marks chiefly add relief.

Final review at 100 marks: broad filled shell planes and short curved shoulders read; six legs remain separated, the compact shoulder reflection holds, and bark/leaf details stay quieter. Raised jaw-tip repair, pointed head, angular joints and regular bristles remain. The final bark neighbor shortened a crowded split in color but left relief. I will stop because further covers are mostly adding ridges.

inspiration.title: Natural History Museum stag beetle account
inspiration.interpretation: Imagined beetle on diagonal weathered wood with moss and one fallen gold leaf; no finished composition copied. Woodland Trust source was first considered but fetch returned403; NHM read successfully. Kingfisher rejected after archive match.

creation.practiceGoal: Broad filled wing-case planes, reserved limb and jaw spaces, compact shell reflections.
creation.inspectionEvidence: 27 review boundaries. 26 saved settled cropped whole/2x-close pairs from8 onward;4 whole screenshot shows canvas but4 close screenshot clips lower canvas, retained as framing limitation.
